summary: Proposes a non-standard protocol for reliable communication, usable at the second or third level. It considers errors from garbled, lost or misdelivered messages, and discusses ways to improve throughput. The author does not aim to propose a new standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC proposes ways to detect damaged, missing or unexpected messages and recover from them. It uses checks, sequence numbers, replies and retransmission, while noting that perfect transfer cannot be guaranteed.

questions: how to achieve reliable communication on the arpanet
how did early protocols handle message errors
how do you detect lost messages
how do you recover from transmission errors
subtitle: A non-standard proposal for detecting and recovering from message errors.

tldr.problem: Messages can be garbled, lost or arrive when they are not expected, and no protocol can make a channel perfectly error-free.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal combines error checks, sequence numbers, replies, timeouts and retransmission, with an optional limit on how many messages may be outstanding.
tldr.outcome: The RFC presents techniques whose reliability can be improved at a cost, and explicitly describes the proposal as non-standard.

facts.label: Sequence field loss detection
facts.value: Modulo N can detect up to N-1 successive message losses

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 203 as Unknown and records no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. The text explicitly describes its proposal as non-standard.

sections.title: Detecting Different Errors
sections.content:
The RFC divides transmission errors into messages that are lost and messages that arrive unexpectedly. A bit error can cause either kind. Parity bits, checksums or other redundant coding can help detect garbled message contents.

Sequence numbers help a receiver check whether a message could follow the previous one. A modulo-N sequence field can detect up to N-1 successive message losses. A receiver must infer loss from later messages or from a message that is overdue.
sections.plainLanguage: Checks such as parity or checksums can reveal damaged contents. Sequence numbers can show when messages arrive out of order or when one may be missing.

sections.title: Replies, Timeouts and Retransmission
sections.content:
The simplest recovery scheme replies to every accepted message, discards uncorrectable or out-of-sequence messages, and retransmits the last message if no reply arrives within N time units. It sends no new message until the previous one is acknowledged, so only one message is in transit at a time.

To improve throughput, the RFC proposes allowing up to L unreplied messages. If a reply does not arrive in time, messages from the oldest unreplied message onward are retransmitted. A larger L can increase throughput, but also makes recovery more costly.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender can wait for a reply before sending the next message, then resend after a timeout. Sending several messages before waiting can improve throughput, but makes recovery more involved.

sections.title: Starting and Ending a Transfer
sections.content:
The RFC identifies unresolved questions about the first sequence number and how to mark the last message in a finite transfer. Its proposed rules let the first message be repeated until K identical replies arrive, then adjust sequence state. A sender stops retransmitting the last unreplied message after J seconds.

The author notes a race if the network fails for J seconds, because a missing reply may mean either channel failure or the end of a conversation. The proposal says J should be less than N times K.
sections.plainLanguage: Repeated first messages and replies help the two sides agree that a transfer has started. At the end, a timeout can stop retries, but a long outage may be hard to distinguish from a finished conversation.
